items.title: First time court appearance: What not to do
items.summary: We all carry our fair share of courtroom mishaps, particularly from the early years. While mistakes can happen at any stage of the litigation career, the shaking and trembling hits very differently to the newly robed, often accompanied by a strong conviction that the legal career is over and it’s time to relocate to another country. To celebrate these mandatory rites of passage, I polled my litigation circle and discovered these gems. 1. During my first year, I was sent to seek a simple passover before a Supreme Court bench with clear instructions to say “my senior is on his legs in another courtroom”. But of course, appearing before a Supreme Court bench, my overwhelm got the better of me and being painfully honest, I blurted out, “my senior is on his legs in the NCLT” . At this point, I was not aware of the unwritten rule of forum hierarchy. I got a well-deserved chewing out from my senior at this point. - 23 y/o advocate assisting a well sought after criminal lawyer in Delhi. 2. A towering 6ft+ young advocate dropped to one knee in open court at the Supreme Court to catch his senior’s whispered instructions. The judge leaned forward: “Counsel, are you being knighted?” - the 34 y/o senior whispering the instructions, one of the most popular criminal lawyers in the country. 3. While waiting for my matter in the Punjab and Haryana High Court, a young counsel stepped up to request some time, stating that his arguing counsel was currently “on his legs” . When the judge pressed for details on which courtroom the senior was appearing in, the young advocate candidly explained that the senior was currently walking from his car. Hence strictly speaking, he was on his legs at that moment. - 25 y/o visiting advocate waiting to take a pass over herself. 4. Advocate: “My Lords may take up the matter day after yesterday.” Judge: “Day after yesterday?” Advocate: “Apologies, My Lord, day after today.” - 24 y/o junior to a Sr. Adv. in Punjab and Haryana High Court. 5. items.title: Delhi High Court pulls up Delhi government over shortage of doctors, qualified staff in city hospitals
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday pulled up the Delhi government for not recruiting the necessary qualified doctors and staff at government hospitals. A bench of Justice Prathiba M Singh and Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora noted that due to the inadequate recruitment of qualified staff, valuable equipment was also going unused. "There are no technicians running these equipments. The court is completely dissatisfied with the report placed on record. The hospitals are facing enormous difficulty in recruiting the necessary doctors and the staff. There is no uniform HR policy of the Delhi Government," the Court said. Justice Prathiba M Singh and Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora The Court went on to observe, “ Judges will come, judges will go, but the hospitals have to function ." The Court was hearing a suo motu case in which it routinely monitors healthcare services in the city's government hospitals. On August 7 , the Court had expressed shock after being informed that 400 ventilators and 910 oxygen concentrators are lying unused at Guru Teg Bahadur (GTB) Hospital. The Court, in response, had directed the Secretary of the Department of Health and Family Welfare under Delhi government to hold a meeting regarding the recruitment of staff for operating such equipment. In yesterday's hearing of the matter, the Court expressed dissatisfaction over the poor progress made since then. "It does not appear that after the meeting had taken place on August 13, any recruitment has happened," the Court said. It has now directed the Secretary of the Health Department to hold a fresh meeting with each hospital on the issue of recruitment. "The Secretary, Health would have to deal with this issue in a centralised manner rather than allowing recruitment at a local level on a contractual basis. A strict timeline has to be prescribed in a centralised manner even for recruitment on a contractual basis, failing which the hospitals do not seem to be recruiting the necessary staff," the Court stated. Meanwhile, following an interaction with a doctor, the Court noted that there are varying interpretations on constitutes unused equipment at hospitals. The Court indicated that it will delve into such aspects later, and that recruitment issues would have to be prioritised. "First we have to focus on the staff, then we have to focus on the equipment. items.title: Third IIT Bombay suicide this year puts student pressure under spotlight
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A Dalit B.Tech student at the Department of Energy Sciences and Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (IIT-B) died by suicide on Friday, September 18, in what is the third such suicide this year at the campus. 19-year-old Sahil Wakode from Maharashtra’s Yavatmal district was accused of using his phone to cheat in the midterm exam conducted on Friday. He was found unresponsive in his room at Hostel No. 4 on the campus by hostelmates later in the evening. The campus has since erupted in demonstrations by students, with an impromptu protest occurring upon the discovery of the body and carrying on through the night. A protest call was given on the morning of September 19, and students assembled at the site in the face of police barricades. Sahil’s parents reached the campus on September 19, demanding a CID probe into their son's death and alleging caste-based discrimination at the institution as having played a major role. “My son has been tortured. I will file a complaint. I need justice for my child,” his mother told reporters. Later in the day, the Mumbai police registered an FIR in the death of Sahil. The complaint names Prof Suryanarayana Doolla – an IIT-B faculty member and the invigilator who called out Sahil for cheating in the exams – as an accused along with others on charges of abetment of suicide. The police have also applied the Prevention of Atrocities Act after Sahil’s father made a complaint that his son had been subjected to casteist slurs. IIT-B released a statement saying that Sahil was reassured by the Head of the Department that no severe action would be taken against him and that no undue pressure was placed on the student. “No disciplinary action was initiated against the student. The matter was also discussed with the student by the instructor and the Head of the Department, who counselled him and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career,” the statement said. items.title: Warangal airport land acquired, CM Revanth Reddy asks public to suggest names
items.summary: Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy announced that the land acquisition for the long-pending Warangal airport has been fully completed and handed over to the Airports Authority of India (AAI). He invited suggestions from the public on what to name the new airport in Warangal’s Mamnoor. Union Minister for Civil Aviation K Rammohan Naidu had previously said that the airport could be completed in 30 months once the state government handed over the required land to AAI. On September 14, AAI floated a tender worth Rs 213.59 crore for the development of the Warangal airport, with works including construction of a new domestic terminal building, an Air Traffic Control Tower cum Technical Block, Fire Station, and other associated works. “This is not just an airport. It is a new gateway for industry, tourism, education, jobs and investment,” CM Revanth said. Telangana currently has only one operational airport, the Rajiv Gandhi International Airport (RGIA) in Hyderabad. The Mamnoor airport in Warangal has remained defunct for decades and attempts to revive it have been ongoing for years since the Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) was in power. While 696 acres of land at Mamnoor was already with the AAI, the Telangana government had sanctioned Rs 295 crore to acquire another 280 acres. The new airport will be located at a distance of less than 150 km from the existing Shamshabad airport near Hyderabad, for which a no-objection certificate had to be obtained from the GMR Hyderabad International Airport Limited (GHIAL). Another defunct pre-independence era airstrip in Adilabad is also proposed to be developed as a defence airport, with an enclave for civil operations.
